title: Recovering and reversing commits
explanation:
Two different problems, two different tools.

**Undo a commit that others already have → `git revert <commit>`.** It creates a *new* commit that applies the inverse of the old one's changes, so history only moves forward and nobody's copy is invalidated. It needs a clean working tree. `--no-edit` accepts the default message without opening an editor.

**Undo a local, unpushed commit → `git reset`.** `git reset --soft HEAD~1` moves the branch back one commit and leaves that commit's changes staged, ready to recommit — effectively undoing the last `git commit` command.

**Find something you "lost" → the reflog.** Git records where `HEAD` and your branch tips have been. Anything that was committed can almost always be recovered — even commits on deleted branches or replaced by `--amend` — by finding its old id in `git reflog` and pointing a branch at it.

```bash
git revert --no-edit 1a2b3c4    # public: add an inverse commit
git reset --soft HEAD~1         # private: un-commit, keep changes staged
git reflog                      # where has HEAD been? find the lost id
git branch rescue HEAD@{2}      # put a branch on it so it can't get lost again
```
keyIdeas: `git revert` adds a new inverse commit — safe for shared history.
`git reset --soft HEAD~1` un-commits but keeps the changes staged.
The reflog remembers where HEAD and branches have been.
Committed work is almost always recoverable; uncommitted work often is not.

workedExample.problem: Two problems in one repository: (1) the published commit `Raise prices` must be undone without rewriting history; (2) you accidentally `git reset --hard` away a local commit `Add cocoa` and need it back.
steps: (1) Find the commit's id and run `git revert --no-edit <id>`: a new commit restores the old prices, and the commit count goes up by one.
(2) After the mistaken hard reset, the commit is no longer on the branch — but the reflog still lists it.
Look it up in the reflog (`HEAD@{1}` is where HEAD was before the reset) and create a branch there: `git branch rescue HEAD@{1}`.
Verify the rescued branch contains the lost change.

Run it in a throwaway folder:
```sh
git init -q -b trunk shop && cd shop
printf 'tea 3\n' > prices.md && git add prices.md && git commit -q -m 'Add prices'
printf 'tea 9\n' > prices.md && git commit -q -am 'Raise prices'
raise=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git revert --no-edit "$raise" > /dev/null
[ "$(cat prices.md)" = 'tea 3' ]
[ "$(git rev-list --count HEAD)" -eq 3 ]   # history grew; nothing rewritten
printf 'cocoa\n' > menu.md && git add menu.md && git commit -q -m 'Add cocoa'
git reset -q --hard HEAD~1                       # oops
[ ! -e menu.md ]
git reflog -3
git branch rescue 'HEAD@{1}'
[ "$(git log -1 --format=%s rescue)" = 'Add cocoa' ]
echo recovered
```
workedExample.answer: The revert adds a third commit that restores `tea 3`; after the bad hard reset, `git branch rescue 'HEAD@{1}'` brings `Add cocoa` back from the reflog.

pitfalls: Using `git reset` on commits teammates already pulled — revert instead.
Panicking after a bad reset or rebase: check the reflog before doing anything else.
Expecting the reflog to save uncommitted edits — it only tracks commits that refs pointed at.

citations.quote: Given one or more existing commits, revert the changes that the related patches introduce, and record some new commits that record them. This requires your working tree to be clean
Note: git revert is used to record some new commits to reverse the effect of some earlier commits (often only a faulty one).
With this option, git revert will not start the commit message editor.
With reset --soft, it will simply stop there. Now take a second to look at that diagram and realize what happened: it essentially undid the last git commit command.
Remember, anything that is committed in Git can almost always be recovered.
Even commits that were on branches that were deleted or commits that were overwritten with an --amend commit can be recovered
we could get it back by looking at our reflog
However, anything you lose that was never committed is likely never to be seen again.
